Carpal Fractures & Dislocations

Scaphoid Fractures · Perilunate Injuries · Carpal Instability · Radiocarpal Dislocations
AO/OTA 72 Herbert Classification Mayfield Stages Herzberg Classification Ch 44 · R&G 10e

Overview

Epidemiology

  • Carpal fractures account for 18% of all hand fractures
  • The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone (60–70% of carpal fractures), followed by the triquetrum (~14%)
  • Peak incidence in young males aged 20–30 years; typically from sports or falls
  • Perilunate dislocations are frequently missed — up to 25% missed on initial presentation
  • Scaphoid fracture distribution: 70–80% waist, 10–20% proximal pole, 5–10% distal pole/tuberosity

Mechanism of Injury

  • Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) with wrist in dorsiflexion >95° and ulnar deviation
  • Axial load transmitted through the capitate onto the scaphoid waist
  • Perilunate injuries: high-energy wrist hyperextension, ulnar deviation, and intercarpal supination — progressive perilunar instability described by Mayfield stages I–IV
  • Radiocarpal dislocations: extreme force, typically associated with radial styloid fractures

Clinical Evaluation

  • Anatomical snuffbox tenderness — sensitivity ~90%, specificity ~40% for scaphoid fracture
  • Scaphoid tubercle tenderness — palpate volarly at the base of the thenar eminence
  • Watson (scaphoid shift) test — examiner applies pressure on scaphoid tuberosity while wrist is moved from ulnar to radial deviation; a painful clunk with dorsal scaphoid subluxation suggests SL ligament injury
  • Axial compression of the thumb (longitudinal grind test)
  • Assess median nerve function — acute carpal tunnel syndrome in up to 25% of perilunate dislocations
Watson (scaphoid shift) test — pressure on scaphoid tuberosity during radial deviation provokes dorsal subluxation in SL instability. (Rockwood & Green 10e, Ch 44)

Imaging

  • Scaphoid series — four views: PA, true lateral, radial oblique (45° pronation), and ulnar oblique (45° supination)
  • PA with wrist in ulnar deviation elongates the scaphoid, improving fracture detection
  • Ziter view — additional clenched-fist PA view to stress the SL interval
  • CT scan — gold standard for fracture displacement measurement; sagittal cuts along scaphoid long axis
  • MRI — highest sensitivity for occult fractures (approaching 100%); also assesses AVN (proximal pole signal changes) and ligament injuries
Fig 44-10. Four scaphoid views (PA, lateral, radial oblique, ulnar oblique). (R&G 10e)
Fig 44-11. Ziter view for scaphoid fracture diagnosis. (R&G 10e)

Key Radiographic Parameters

Gilula Lines

Three smooth arcs on PA radiograph outlining the proximal and distal surfaces of the proximal carpal row and the proximal cortical margins of the capitate and hamate. Disruption of any arc suggests carpal malalignment or dislocation.

Fig 44-12. Gilula lines — Arc I disruption in perilunate dislocation. (R&G 10e)

Carpal Height Ratio

Ratio of carpal height (L2) to third metacarpal length (L1). Normal: 0.54 ± 0.03. Decreased ratio indicates carpal collapse (DISI, SNAC, SLAC).

Fig 44-13. Carpal-height ratio = L2/L1. (R&G 10e)

Scapholunate Angle

Measured on true lateral radiograph. Normal: 30–60°. DISI: >60° (lunate dorsiflexed, scaphoid volar flexed). VISI: <30° (lunate volar flexed).

Fig 44-14. SL angle — long axis of scaphoid vs. perpendicular to capitolunate axis. (R&G 10e)

DISI & VISI Patterns

DISI: SL angle >60°, CL angle >15°; lunate tilts dorsally, scaphoid flexes volarly. Associated with SL ligament disruption. VISI: SL angle <30°, CL angle >30°; lunate tilts volarly. Associated with LT ligament disruption.

Fig 44-15. Normal alignment (A), DISI (B), VISI (C). (R&G 10e)

Anatomy

Carpal Bones

The carpus is composed of eight bones arranged in two rows that provide motion and transfer forces from the hand to the forearm.

  • Proximal row: scaphoid (S), lunate (L), triquetrum (T), pisiform (P — sesamoid within FCU tendon)
  • Distal row: trapezium (Tm), trapezoid (Td), capitate (C), hamate (H)
  • The proximal row functions as an intercalated segment — no tendon insertions, motion entirely dictated by articular geometry and ligamentous constraints
Fig 44-1. PA radiograph — two rows of carpal bones: S=scaphoid, L=lunate, T=triquetrum, P=pisiform, C=capitate, H=hamate, Td=trapezoid, Tm=trapezium. (R&G 10e)

Carpal Kinematics

Multiple models describe carpal motion:

  • Column theory: lateral column (scaphoid, trapezium, trapezoid), central column (lunate, capitate, hamate), medial column (triquetrum, pisiform)
  • Oval ring theory: proximal and distal rows form an oval ring; disruption at any point creates instability
  • Row theory: proximal and distal rows function as units with the proximal row as an intercalated segment
Fig 44-5. Columnar theory of carpal kinematics. (R&G 10e)
Fig 44-6. Oval (A) and row (B) theories. (R&G 10e)

Ligamentous Anatomy

Extrinsic Ligaments

Connect radius/ulna to the carpus. Divide into palmar (stronger) and dorsal groups:

  • Palmar extrinsic: radioscaphocapitate (RSC), long radiolunate (LRL), short radiolunate (SRL), radioscapholunate (ligament of Testut — actually a neurovascular structure), ulnolunate, ulnotriquetral
  • Dorsal extrinsic: dorsal radiocarpal (DRC) and dorsal intercarpal (DIC) ligaments — form a "V" pattern converging on the triquetrum
  • The space of Poirier is a weak area of the volar capsule between the RSC and LRL ligaments — site of carpal dislocation
Fig 44-2. A: Extrinsic palmar ligaments. B: Extrinsic dorsal ligaments of the carpus. (R&G 10e)

Intrinsic Ligaments

Connect carpal bones to one another. The most clinically important are:

  • Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) — the most critical carpal stabilizer; dorsal component is strongest; disruption leads to DISI pattern
  • Lunotriquetral interosseous ligament (LTIL) — palmar component is strongest; disruption leads to VISI pattern
  • Midcarpal intrinsic ligaments: scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT), scaphocapitate (SC), triquetrocapitate (TC), triquetrohamate (TH)
Fig 44-3. A: Palmar intrinsic ligaments. B: Dorsal intrinsic ligaments. Key: SL=scapholunate, LT=lunotriquetral, STT=scaphotrapeziotrapezoid, SC=scaphocapitate. (R&G 10e)

Vascular Supply

Carpal Blood Supply

The carpus receives blood from the radial, ulnar, and anterior interosseous arteries via three dorsal and three palmar arterial arches:

  • Palmar radiocarpal arch, palmar intercarpal arch, deep palmar arch
  • Dorsal radiocarpal arch, dorsal intercarpal arch, basal metacarpal arch
Fig 44-4. Arterial supply of the palmar carpus: 1=palmar radiocarpal arch, 2=palmar branch AIA, 3=palmar intercarpal arch, 4=deep palmar arch, 5=recurrent artery. (R&G 10e)

Scaphoid Blood Supply

Critical for understanding fracture healing and AVN risk:

  • Supplied by two pedicles from the radial artery: dorsal branch (enters dorsal ridge at waist — supplies 70–80% of intraosseous vascularity including entire proximal pole) and volar branch (enters distal tuberosity — supplies distal 20–30%)
  • Blood supply is retrograde to the proximal pole — waist and proximal pole fractures disrupt perfusion
  • AVN risk: ~30% for proximal pole fractures, ~10–20% for waist fractures
  • ~80% of the scaphoid surface is covered by articular cartilage, leaving limited area for vascular entry
Fig 44-17. Scaphoid vascular supply — dorsal and volar pedicles from the radial artery. The dorsal branch supplies the proximal pole in a retrograde fashion. (R&G 10e)
Clinical Pearl: The dorsal branch of the radial artery enters the scaphoid at the dorsal ridge (waist level). Fractures at or proximal to this entry point compromise the retrograde blood supply to the proximal pole, explaining the high rates of nonunion and AVN with proximal pole fractures.

Classification

Herbert & Fisher Classification (Scaphoid Fractures)

The most widely used system for scaphoid fractures. Divides into four categories based on stability and chronicity:

Fig 44-21. Herbert & Fisher classification of scaphoid fractures: Type A (stable), B (unstable), C (delayed union), D (nonunion). (R&G 10e)

Mayfield Stages — Progressive Perilunate Instability

Describes the progressive arc of ligamentous disruption in perilunate injuries. Force propagates from radial to ulnar around the lunate:

Fig 44-35. Mayfield stages I–IV of progressive perilunate instability. (R&G 10e)

Herzberg Classification (Perilunate Dislocations)

Classifies perilunate injuries by whether the injury arc passes through ligaments alone (lesser arc) or through bone (greater arc):

  • Lesser arc — pure ligamentous disruption
  • Greater arc — trans-osseous fractures (trans-scaphoid, trans-capitate, trans-radial styloid, trans-triquetral)

Management

Scaphoid Fractures

Non-operative Treatment

  • Indications: Herbert A1 (tuberosity) and A2 (incomplete waist) fractures; non-displaced, stable waist fractures with <1 mm displacement on CT
  • Short-arm thumb spica cast (below-elbow), wrist in slight extension, thumb IP joint free
  • Duration: 6 weeks for tuberosity fractures, 8–12 weeks for waist fractures
  • Serial radiographs at 2-week intervals to confirm alignment and healing
  • If no radiographic evidence of healing at 6 weeks → CT to assess union
  • Expected union rate: >95% for non-displaced waist fractures with adequate immobilization
AO Foundation Recommendation: Below-elbow circumferential cast with wrist in slight dorsiflexion. Cast molding over the scaphoid tuberosity (volarly) and capitate (dorsally) can help reduce subtle displacement. The cast must allow full MCP and thumb IP joint motion.

Operative Treatment — Scaphoid ORIF

  • Indications for surgery:
    • Displacement >1 mm gap or step-off on CT
    • SL angle >60°
    • Radiolunate angle >15°
    • Intrascaphoid angle >35°
    • All proximal pole fractures (Herbert B3)
    • Fracture-dislocations (Herbert B4)
    • Comminuted fractures (Herbert B5)
    • Associated carpal instability
  • Fixation: headless compression screw (e.g., Herbert, Acutrak, Synthes HCS) placed along the central axis of the scaphoid
  • Approach selection: volar for distal third/waist fractures; dorsal for waist/proximal pole; percutaneous techniques available for both
  • Post-op: short-arm thumb spica splint for 2 weeks, then removable orthosis for 4–6 weeks, progressive ROM

Scaphoid Nonunion

  • Defined as no healing at ≥6 months from injury
  • Treatment depends on presence of AVN, carpal collapse (humpback deformity), and arthritis:
  • Without AVN: headless compression screw + cancellous bone graft (iliac crest or distal radius)
  • With AVN but no arthritis: vascularized bone graft — 1,2-intercompartmental supraretinacular artery (1,2-ICSRA) pedicled graft from distal radius (Zaidemberg) or free medial femoral condyle graft
  • With SNAC/SLAC arthritis: salvage procedures — scaphoid excision + four-corner fusion, proximal row carpectomy, or total wrist arthrodesis

Perilunate Dislocations

Surgical Emergency: All perilunate and lunate dislocations require urgent operative treatment. Median nerve compression occurs in up to 25% of cases — assess and document nerve function before and after reduction. Emergent closed reduction should be performed in the ED.
  • Emergency reduction: longitudinal traction with wrist extension, then flexion while maintaining traction. Thumb pressure on lunate volarly to reduce it back into the lunate fossa
  • Definitive treatment: open reduction via combined dorsal and volar approach
    • Dorsal approach: reduce carpal alignment, repair SL and LT ligaments, fix any fractures (trans-scaphoid, trans-radial styloid)
    • Volar approach: carpal tunnel release, decompress median nerve, repair volar capsular ligaments (space of Poirier), address lunate reduction
    • K-wire fixation: SL, SC, ± LT wires for 8–12 weeks
  • Greater arc injuries: ORIF of all fractures (scaphoid with headless screw, radial styloid with lag screw or K-wires) + ligament repair
  • Post-op: above-elbow sugar-tong splint for 2 weeks → short-arm cast for 6 weeks → K-wire removal at 8–12 weeks → progressive ROM

Radiocarpal Dislocations

  • Rare, high-energy injuries; often associated with radial styloid fractures
  • Treatment: dorsal spanning plate + volar ligamentous repair; K-wire augmentation of radiocarpal alignment
  • If large radial styloid fragment: ORIF with buttress plate or lag screws
Fig 44-50. Radiocarpal dislocation with radial styloid fracture — pre-op (A, B) and post-op (C, D) with dorsal spanning plate and volar repair. (R&G 10e)

Surgical Approaches

Volar Approach to Scaphoid (FCR Approach)

  • Indication: distal third and waist fractures, Matti-Russe bone grafting, volar plating for nonunion
  • Interval: along the FCR tendon; retract FCR ulnarly
  • Incise floor of FCR sheath to expose scaphoid tuberosity and volar waist
  • Structures at risk: radial artery (lateral to FCR), palmar cutaneous branch of median nerve
  • Allows direct visualization of the scaphoid tuberosity and distal pole for screw insertion

Dorsal Approach to Scaphoid

  • Indication: proximal pole fractures, dorsal percutaneous screw fixation, vascularized bone graft harvest (1,2-ICSRA)
  • Interval: between 3rd (EPL) and 4th (EDC) extensor compartments, centered on Lister tubercle
  • EPL retracted radially; dorsal capsulotomy in ligament-sparing fashion
  • Wrist flexion brings proximal pole into view for central guidewire placement
  • Structures at risk: dorsal branch of radial artery, posterior interosseous nerve (may be excised for denervation)

Combined Dorsal-Volar Approach (Perilunate Injuries)

Preferred Approach for Perilunate Dislocations: A combined dorsal and volar approach is the standard of care for definitive treatment of perilunate injuries. The dorsal approach allows reduction and ligament repair; the volar approach allows carpal tunnel decompression and volar capsular repair.
  • Dorsal approach (first):
    • Longitudinal incision centered on Lister tubercle
    • 3rd/4th compartment interval; capsulotomy
    • Reduce carpal alignment under direct visualization and fluoroscopy
    • Repair dorsal SL and LT ligaments with suture anchors
    • ORIF of any fractures (trans-scaphoid with HCS)
    • K-wire fixation: SL and SC wires minimum; ± LT wire
  • Volar approach (second):
    • Extended carpal tunnel incision
    • Release transverse carpal ligament — decompress median nerve
    • Repair volar capsular ligaments (space of Poirier closure)
    • Assess and repair short radiolunate and radioscaphocapitate ligaments
    • Confirm lunate reduction

Complications

Scaphoid Fracture Complications

Nonunion

  • Overall nonunion rate: 5–10% for appropriately treated acute fractures
  • Risk factors: proximal pole location, displacement >1 mm, delayed presentation (>4 weeks), smoking, inadequate immobilization
  • Untreated nonunion → progressive humpback deformity (flexion of distal fragment) → DISI → SNAC wrist (scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse)
  • SNAC wrist arthritic progression: Stage I (radial styloid–scaphoid), Stage II (scaphocapitate), Stage III (capitolunate), Stage IV (pancarpal)

Avascular Necrosis (AVN)

  • Incidence: ~30–40% proximal pole fractures, ~10–20% waist fractures
  • Due to retrograde blood supply from dorsal branch of radial artery
  • MRI is the gold standard — assess proximal pole signal on T1/T2
  • Proximal pole sclerosis on plain radiographs suggests AVN
  • Treatment: vascularized bone graft (1,2-ICSRA or free medial femoral condyle) if no arthritis; salvage if arthritis present

Malunion

  • Intrascaphoid angulation → humpback deformity → altered carpal mechanics
  • Loss of wrist extension and grip strength
  • Treatment: corrective osteotomy with wedge grafting to restore scaphoid anatomy

Perilunate Dislocation Complications

Median Nerve Injury

  • Acute carpal tunnel syndrome in up to 25% of perilunate/lunate dislocations
  • Due to direct compression by dislocated lunate or carpal swelling
  • Requires urgent carpal tunnel release at time of definitive surgery

Post-traumatic Arthritis

  • Develops in ~50% of perilunate injuries despite adequate treatment
  • Radiocarpal and midcarpal arthritis from chondral damage at time of injury
  • May progress to SLAC wrist pattern (scapholunate advanced collapse)
  • SLAC progression: Stage I (radial styloid–scaphoid), Stage II (radioscaphoid), Stage III (capitolunate)

Stiffness & Loss of Motion

  • Universal after perilunate injuries — expect 50–60% of normal wrist ROM
  • Grip strength typically recovers to ~80% of contralateral
  • Early ROM after K-wire removal (8–12 weeks) improves outcomes

Chronic Carpal Instability

  • SL ligament attenuation despite repair → recurrent DISI
  • SL interval widening (>3 mm) persists in many patients
  • Secondary procedures: tenodesis (Brunelli, 3-ligament tenodesis), capsulodesis, SL screw, or SL arthrodesis
